title: Anthropic to build in-house chip design team for Claude, hire engineers
author: B
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Anthropic, a U.S.-based artificial intelligence firm, is creating an internal chip design team to build custom hardware for its Claude AI models. The move comes as AI companies face growing demand for advanced computing power and seek more control over the technology needed to train and run large AI systems.

Anthropic said it is hiring engineers with experience across hardware and software development to help design in-house AI chips that can make Claude run faster and more efficiently. The company wants to create hardware that is better suited to its AI models while improving performance for users.

As part of the effort, Anthropic stated that custom silicon will become a key part of its broader multi-chip strategy. However, the company said it will keep relying on tech from Amazon , Google, Nvidia and AMD.

Meanwhile, the Claude creator’s hiring activity suggests it is taking a long-term approach to building its own AI chips. The company is already recruiting engineers for its custom silicon team, with job roles offering annual pay between $320,000 and $485,000.

Despite the hiring push, the company has also not yet disclosed when its chips will be ready or whether it plans to handle manufacturing itself.

Anthropic’s chip ambitions reflect a wider trend in the AI industry, where many AI companies are exploring custom hardware to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, whose GPUs currently lead the market.

Building custom chips allows AI firms to create hardware made for their own AI models, which could improve speed and lower computing costs over time. However, the process is costly and complex, with advanced AI chip development often needing hundreds of millions of dollars due to design costs, testing and production issues.

Like Anthropic, other major AI companies have also been pursuing similar custom chip plans. OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, recently partnered with chipmaker Broadcom on a homegrown AI chip project. Meanwhile, global tech giant Meta Platforms is developing next-generation AI hardware. Even French AI startup Mistral AI has been linked to efforts to explore custom chip development.

For investors, the move shows that competition in the AI sector is expanding beyond open-source models. Companies are now trying harder to control more of the technology stack, including the chips that power their systems, as access to computing resources becomes a key factor in the AI race.
